KEY MESSAGE 1...As of 3:10 AM EDT...Current GOES 16 WV imagery 
shows a strong upper trough with multiple embedded shortwaves 
digging into the Great Lakes. At the sfc, a 990 mb sfc low is 
currently tracking towards James Bay. This is resulting in 
mainly cloudy skies across our region. Temperatures are mainly 
in the 50s to 60s, and are not expected to drop much from 
current levels through the remainder of the night. 

This morning, the sfc low will lift a mid-level warm front through 
the region, although the sfc warm front remains hung up to our south 
until later this afternoon when southern areas finally get into a 
narrow warm sector. We will see scattered showers and perhaps some 
elevated thunderstorms with the mid-level warm advection/isentropic 
lift this morning, followed by additional chances for showers and 
storms this afternoon into early tonight with and ahead of a weak 
cold front and associated wind shift boundary. 

While some strong to severe storms are possible today (see next 
paragraph), the bigger threat if fact appears to be locally heavy 
rain. PWAT values increase to around 2" by this afternoon, with warm 
cloud depths of around 12 kft allowing for very efficient warm rain 
processes. Storm motions do look fast, but multiple rounds of storms 
are possible today. Additionally, flow aloft parallel to the 
approaching boundary will allow for backbuilding and training of 
storms, especially this afternoon. The heavy rain threat looks 
greatest for the Mid Hudson Valley, southeastern Catskills, and 
possibly the western Mohawk Valley/southern ADKs. 00z HREF does show 
a small area with a 30% chance for >3" of rain in 3 hrs this 
afternoon across the Mid Hudson Valley, which is usually a decent 
signal for potential hydro issues. There was some consideration 
given to a flood watch for our southern row of counties, but we 
decided to hold off in coordination with neighboring offices 
given most areas are still in a rainfall deficit and FFG values
are fairly high. WPC did add the Mid Hudson Valley, southeastern
Catskills, and southwestern New England into the slight risk 
ERO, which makes sense given the environment. Main concern would
be for any urban areas, but some ponding of water and isolated 
flash flooding will still be possible anywhere that sees 
training and backbuilding of storms. 

There is also a severe weather threat today. For the western 
Mohawk Valley, southeastern Catskills, and Mid Hudson Valley the
warm front is expected to lift north of these areas this 
afternoon/early evening, allowing for up to around 1000 J/kg of 
SBCAPE. Strong low-level and deep layers shear with elongated, 
curved hodographs suggests the potential here for a few right- 
moving supercells. Main concern would be damaging winds, but an 
isolated tornado can't be ruled out with low LCLs and impressive
veering wind profile. Can't totally rule out some large hail 
with any supercells either. However, instability looks much more
limited for areas further north and east due to the slow 
advancement of the warm front and widespread cloud cover/showers
around through much of the morning. Additionally, there will be
a capping inversion in place and the best forcing (sfc cold 
front and upper-level support) doesn't arrive until after peak 
diurnal heating. Therefore, severe weather potential looks 
lower today outside of the western Mohawk Valley, southeastern 
Catskills, and Mid Hudson Valley. SPC has maintained their 
slight risk for severe today across all but the upper Hudson 
Valley, southern VT, and the Berkshires, although the 
northeastern extent of the slight risk seems overly aggressive 
given the lack of instability and numerous other limiting 
factors. 

Showers and storms likely linger into tonight, but should diminish 
in coverage especially after midnight. On Wednesday, a second, 
stronger cold front will track through the region. For most of our 
area, the frontal passage will be too early for any severe weather, 
but there is a low chance for western New England with the front 
slowing down as it tracks further east. Threat for severe is very 
conditional as unimpressive mid-level lapse rates and abundant 
mid- level dry air will be very tough to overcome, but if 
convection can get going then shear is impressive, with 
hodographs suggesting splitting cells and even dominant left 
movers would be possible. SPC has trimmed back the western 
extent of the marginal risk from the previous forecast as the 
timing of the frontal passage looks slightly earlier.

air will filter into the region Wednesday into Wednesday night.
SFC high pressure building overhead should promote quiet 
weather conditions despite broad upper troughing aloft. Thursday
will be quite comfortable with highs in the 70s and lows in the
